hunt.justification: Passkeys are highly secure, but as the Huntress research shows, attackers are pivoting to the enrollment and recovery lifecycles. A negative result verifies that our move to passkeys is not being undermined by parallel authentication flows.

meta.name: Passkey-Themed Phishing and Identity Lifecycle Abuse

related.reason: This hunt focuses specifically on the passkey-themed lure vector; broader OAuth abuse is covered separately.

meta.analysis: This hunt is not just a single rule; it connects three distinct signals: an unusual login protocol, an account security modification, and a cloud persistence operation. A single rule firing on any one of these would be high-noise, but the narrative connection across identity and cloud surfaces is what identifies a real compromise.

stages.name: Passkey-Themed Phishing Lures
observables: AI-generated phishing lures tailored to victim roles
Impersonation of IT staff requesting passkey updates
Urgent enrollment requests or messages to authorize unfamiliar devices

stages.name: Abuse of Alternative Auth Flows
observables: Victims entering device codes on legitimate Microsoft login pages
Abuse of OAuth device-code flows to obtain valid sessions

stages.name: Malicious Enrollment and Persistence
observables: Creation of inbox rules or mail forwarding addresses
New OAuth application grants and consents

stages.name: Endpoint Browser Tampering
observables: Unauthorized browser extensions from non-approved lists
Unexpected browser redirects or toolbars during sign-in

scenario.summary: The EvilTokens campaign and similar threats target the account lifecycle by using AI-generated phishing to abuse device-code flows and register malicious authenticators. Even with passkeys, attackers maintain access through unauthorized MFA enrollment, session persistence via OAuth grants, and endpoint-level browser manipulation to intercept authentication responses.

meta.rationale: The hunt should begin with users who have performed Device Code authentication, as this is the primary flow abused in the EvilTokens campaign and is rarely used in standard business operations.
meta.hypothesis: An attacker uses social engineering lures themed around passkey enrollment to trick users into authorizing a device-code login flow, subsequently registering unauthorized authenticators and establishing persistence via cloud application grants or unapproved browser extensions.

blind_spots.question: whether persistence was established before the current log window

blind_spots.risk: Software inventory only shows installed extensions; it cannot see memory-resident hooks injected via other processes, potentially missing advanced browser tampering.

hunt.name: Passkey-Themed Phishing and Identity Lifecycle Abuse
hunt.description: This phased hunt targets the abuse of identity lifecycles during transition to phishing-resistant authentication. The first phase identifies users who use rare alternative authentication flows, such as the Device Code flow seen in the EvilTokens campaign, and correlates this with immediate MFA enrollment changes. The second phase follows these high-risk identities to find post-authentication persistence mechanisms, including malicious inbox rules and unauthorized browser extensions capable of tampering with WebAuthn responses. The hunt concludes by connecting the initial social engineering signal to the technical persistence evidence.

config.content: SELECT actor_user_name, device_hostname, src_endpoint_ip, auth_protocol, time FROM hb_auth_signin WHERE (LOWER(auth_protocol) LIKE '%device%code%' OR LOWER(event_type) LIKE '%device%code%') AND status_id = 1 AND time >= datetime('now', '-{{lookback_days}} days')
config.description: Identify users and hosts that use the Device Code flow, which is a primary vector for session hijacking in passkey-themed phishing campaigns.
config.expected_signal: Rows identify users who successfully authorized a device code flow. In most enterprises, this flow should be rare.

config.description: Detect when a user adds a new authenticator or resets credentials, which often follows a hijacked session.
config.expected_signal: Modifications to account security settings shortly after a login event. Silent means no such changes were recorded.

config.objective: Evaluate whether the early-stage identity risks resulted in cloud persistence (inbox rules/OAuth) or endpoint tampering (unapproved extensions).
config.description: Integrate the early identity signals with the technical persistence mechanisms to verify the full attack lifecycle.

config.success_criteria: A final verdict of malicious or suspicious for each user and host, mapping the timeline of the compromise.

config.question: the full-chain-correlation verdict is malicious for at least one user
config.condition: the full-chain-correlation verdict is malicious for at least one user
config.description: Direct the response based on the agent's full-chain correlation.
Immediately terminate the attacker's access by revoking sessions and removing malicious authenticators.
config.instructions: Revoke all active sessions for the compromised user, remove any authenticators registered during the incident window, and disable unauthorized OAuth application grants.

config.description: Verify that all persistence mechanisms, including inbox rules and browser extensions, have been fully remediated.
config.instructions: Review the compromised mailbox for hidden inbox rules or forwarding addresses. Confirm that the unapproved extensions on the affected host have been uninstalled. Update the approved_extension_ids list if the extension was legitimate.
